Connect to foundations: Stellar structure and the mass–luminosity relation ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A cool photosphere and convective interior A pre-main-sequence star can shine through contraction before nuclear reactions dominate. Approximate a fully convective monatomic ideal-gas interior by an n = 3/2 polytrope. Its surface temperature also requires a boundary condition where light escapes. P = Kρ5/3, P = ℛρT, ℛ ≡ kBμmp K ∝ GM1/3R The last scaling follows by eliminating central density from the n = 3/2 Lane–Emden structure. Hold composition fixed. Partial ionization and a superadiabatic surface layer limit this idealized adiabat. 02Supply a photospheric pressure In a thin plane atmosphere dP/dτ = g/κ. Taking representative g and κ at optical depth about 2/3 gives Pph ≈ 2g/(3κph). Supply an approximate low-temperature H⁻ opacity per unit mass; microscopic opacity theory is outside this chapter. Pph ≈ 2g3κph, g = GMR² κ = κ₀ρaTb, a = 12, b = 7.7 The opacity power law has a limited temperature/composition range, and κ₀ carries units. Approximate the photospheric temperature by effective temperature to connect the atmosphere and interior; do not extrapolate the law to all stars. 03A strong opacity power gives a weak temperature scaling Eliminate density with ρ = P/(ℛT). The adiabat then gives P = (ℛT)⁵ᐟ²K⁻³ᐟ². Substitute into the photospheric condition and collect the powers of K, M and R. Pa+1 ∝ gκ₀−1ℛaTa−b Teff3a+2b+5 ∝ κ₀−2Ma+3R3a−1 Teff ∝ M3.5/21.9R0.5/21.9, ε ≡ 143.8 ≈ 0.02283 L = 4πR²σSBTeff⁴ ∝ R2+4ε (fixed M) A large radius change produces little temperature change, giving a nearly vertical H–R path. The cool boundary is the Hayashi limit. This scaling estimates its slope; it does not replace a detailed atmosphere calculation or establish every forbidden configuration. 04Use luminosity to time contraction Omit nuclear burning, accretion and mass loss, and take total energy E = −3GM²/(7R). Integrating L = −dE/dt gives a contraction law. Write ℓ = 2+4ε and use initial radius R₀ and luminosity L₀. L = −3GM²7R²dRdt, RR₀ = (1+tt₀)−1/(ℓ+1) t₀ = 3GM²7(ℓ+1)R₀L₀ The teaching model chooses R₀ = 3 solar radii and T₀ = 4000 K × (M/M☉)3.5/21.9. The temperature normalization is supplied, not calibrated from κ₀. Main-sequence arrival, radiative-core formation and realistic stellar tracks are not computed. 05Leaving a Hayashi track A radiative interior invalidates a single n = 3/2 convective model. Following a hotter Henyey track requires radiative transport and internal structure. Different nearly vertical curves need not describe the same mass or evolutionary phase. Playback advances the specified energy model. It is more than moving an observational point, but it does not reproduce published numerical tracks. Separate the weak temperature dependence from the energy budget that sets elapsed time. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. With this chapter’s opacity powers, halve radius at fixed mass. How do effective temperature and luminosity change? Show the answer and reasoning With ε = 1/43.8, temperature changes by 2−ε ≈ 0.984 and luminosity by 2−(2+4ε) ≈ 0.235. The small temperature change leaves area as the main luminosity factor. These powers belong to the stated atmosphere approximation, not a detailed evolution calculation. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
